questions.q: Which pair contains only SI base units?
questions.x: The seven SI base units are kg, m, s, A, K, mol and cd. The coulomb (A s), newton (kg m s⁻²) and volt are derived units.

questions.q: The diameter of a cylinder is (2.00 ± 0.02) cm and its length is (5.0 ± 0.1) cm. What is the percentage uncertainty in its volume V = πd²L/4?
A student takes repeated readings that are very close to one another, but their mean is far from the true value. The readings are
o: accurate and precise, with a large random error
accurate but not precise, with a large systematic error
precise but not accurate, with a large systematic error
neither accurate nor precise, with a large random error
questions.x: Small scatter means precise (small random error). A mean far from the true value means inaccurate, which comes from a systematic error such as a zero error.

questions.q: Which list contains only vector quantities?
questions.x: Speed, work and mass are scalars. Momentum, weight (a force) and displacement all have direction.

questions.q: A ball is thrown vertically upwards at 15 m s⁻¹. Air resistance is negligible. What is the maximum height it reaches above the point of release?
questions.x: At the top v = 0, so h = u²/2g = 15²/(2 × 9.81) = 11.5 m.

questions.q: A stone is thrown horizontally at 20 m s⁻¹ from the top of a cliff 45 m high. Air resistance is negligible. How far from the foot of the cliff does it land?
questions.x: Vertical: 45 = ½(9.81)t², so t = 3.03 s. Horizontal: x = 20 × 3.03 = 61 m.

questions.q: A car decelerates uniformly from 30 m s⁻¹ to rest over a distance of 75 m. What is the magnitude of its deceleration?
questions.x: v² = u² + 2as gives 0 = 900 + 2a(75), so a = −6.0 m s⁻².

questions.q: Blocks of mass 2.0 kg and 3.0 kg are in contact on a frictionless floor. A horizontal force of 10 N pushes the 2.0 kg block, which pushes the 3.0 kg block. What force does the 2.0 kg block exert on the 3.0 kg block?
questions.x: a = 10/5.0 = 2.0 m s⁻². The only horizontal force on the 3.0 kg block is the contact force, so F = 3.0 × 2.0 = 6.0 N.

questions.q: A 2.0 kg trolley moving at 3.0 m s⁻¹ collides with a stationary 1.0 kg trolley and they stick together. How much kinetic energy is lost?
questions.x: Momentum: 6.0 = 3.0v, so v = 2.0 m s⁻¹. KE before = 9.0 J, KE after = ½(3.0)(2.0)² = 6.0 J. Loss = 3.0 J.

questions.q: A 0.10 kg ball hits a wall at 8.0 m s⁻¹ and rebounds along the same line at 6.0 m s⁻¹. It is in contact with the wall for 0.020 s. What is the average force on the ball?
questions.x: Velocity reverses, so Δp = 0.10(8.0 + 6.0) = 1.4 N s. F = Δp/Δt = 1.4/0.020 = 70 N.

questions.q: Two objects have a perfectly elastic head-on collision. Which statement is always correct?
o: Each object keeps its own kinetic energy.
The relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation.
The objects move off with equal speeds.
The object with the smaller mass comes to rest.
questions.x: In an elastic collision total KE is conserved. Combined with conservation of momentum, this gives relative speed of approach = relative speed of separation.

questions.q: A uniform horizontal beam 4.0 m long and of weight 200 N is hinged at one end. A 50 N load hangs from the free end. A vertical string attached 3.0 m from the hinge holds the beam horizontal. What is the tension in the string?
questions.x: Moments about the hinge: T(3.0) = 200(2.0) + 50(4.0) = 600 N m, so T = 200 N.

questions.q: A block weighs 5.0 N in air. It hangs from a spring balance fully immersed in water of density 1000 kg m⁻³. Its volume is 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ m³. What does the balance read?
A rigid body is in equilibrium. Which statement must be true?
o: Only two forces act on it, and they are equal and opposite.
The resultant force is zero, but there may be a resultant torque.
The resultant force is zero and the resultant torque about any point is zero.
questions.x: Equilibrium needs both no resultant force (no linear acceleration) and no resultant torque about any point (no angular acceleration). It may move at constant velocity.

questions.q: A 1200 kg car travels at a constant 25 m s⁻¹ on a level road against a total resistive force of 800 N. What useful power does the engine deliver?
questions.x: At constant speed the driving force equals 800 N. P = Fv = 800 × 25 = 20 kW. The mass is not needed.

questions.q: A motor with efficiency 80% lifts a 50 kg load vertically at a constant 0.40 m s⁻¹. What is the input power of the motor?
A 2.0 kg block starts from rest and slides down a rough slope, dropping a vertical height of 5.0 m. It reaches the bottom at 8.0 m s⁻¹. How much work is done against friction?
questions.x: GPE lost = 2.0 × 9.81 × 5.0 = 98.1 J. KE gained = ½(2.0)(8.0)² = 64 J. Work against friction = 98.1 − 64 = 34 J.

questions.q: A 0.20 kg stone on a 0.50 m string moves in a vertical circle. At the top of the circle its speed is 4.0 m s⁻¹. What is the tension in the string there?
What is the angular velocity of the second hand of a clock?
An object moves in a horizontal circle at constant speed. Which quantity stays constant?
questions.x: Velocity, momentum and centripetal acceleration all change direction continuously. Only the magnitude of speed, and so the kinetic energy, is constant.

questions.q: The gravitational field strength at the Earth's surface is g₀. What is it at a height above the surface equal to the Earth's radius?
questions.x: g ∝ 1/r². The distance from the Earth's centre doubles (R → 2R), so g falls to g₀/4.

questions.q: Satellite X orbits a planet with a period 8 times that of satellite Y. What is the ratio (orbital radius of X)/(orbital radius of Y)?
questions.x: Kepler's third law: T² ∝ r³, so r ∝ T^(2/3). 8^(2/3) = 4.

questions.q: The gravitational potential at the surface of a planet is −6.0 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹. Ignoring the atmosphere and the planet's rotation, what is the minimum energy needed to send a 500 kg probe to infinity?
A fixed mass of ideal gas in a sealed rigid container is heated from 27 °C to 127 °C. What is the ratio (final pressure)/(initial pressure)?
questions.x: At constant volume, p ∝ T in kelvin: 400 K / 300 K = 1.33. Using °C (127/27) is the trap.

questions.q: The thermodynamic temperature of an ideal gas is raised from 300 K to 1200 K. By what factor does the r.m.s. speed of its molecules change?
An ideal gas occupies 0.025 m³ at a pressure of 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa and a temperature of 300 K. How many moles of gas are present?
A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on its surroundings. What is the change in its internal energy?
questions.x: ΔU = Q + W, where W is work done ON the gas = −200 J. ΔU = 500 − 200 = +300 J.

questions.q: A 1.0 kW heater warms 0.50 kg of water for 2.0 minutes. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Assuming no heat loss, what is the rise in temperature?
An ideal gas expands slowly at constant temperature. Which statement is correct?
o: Its internal energy increases by the heat supplied.
Its internal energy is unchanged, and the heat supplied equals the work done by the gas.
No heat is exchanged, so the gas cools.
The work done on the gas is positive.
questions.x: The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on T, so ΔU = 0. Then Q = −W: heat in equals work done by the gas as it expands.

questions.q: A particle moves with simple harmonic motion described by x = 0.050 sin(20t), where x is in metres and t in seconds. What is its maximum acceleration?
questions.x: a_max = ω²x₀ = 20² × 0.050 = 20 m s⁻². (1.0 m s⁻¹ is the maximum speed ωx₀.)

questions.q: The mass on a spring oscillating in SHM is replaced with one four times as large. What happens to the period?
questions.x: T = 2π√(m/k), so T ∝ √m. Four times the mass doubles the period.

questions.q: An object performs SHM with amplitude A. What fraction of its total energy is kinetic when its displacement is A/2?
questions.x: PE ∝ x², so at x = A/2 the PE is ¼ of the total. KE = 1 − ¼ = ¾ of the total.

questions.q: A system is driven at various frequencies. Its damping is then increased. How does the amplitude–frequency curve change?
o: The peak becomes higher and sharper.
The peak becomes lower and broader, and moves to a slightly lower frequency.
The peak moves to a much higher frequency with no change in height.
The curve does not change, because damping affects only free oscillations.
questions.x: More damping removes energy faster. Resonance gives a smaller maximum amplitude, a flatter peak, and a peak frequency slightly below the natural frequency.

questions.q: A point source radiates sound uniformly in all directions. The intensity is I at 2.0 m from the source. What is the intensity at 6.0 m?
questions.x: Intensity follows the inverse square law, I ∝ 1/r². Three times the distance gives I/9.

questions.q: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes through two polarisers whose transmission axes are 60° apart. What intensity emerges?
questions.x: The first polariser halves unpolarised light: I₀/2. Malus's law at the second: (I₀/2)cos²60° = (I₀/2)(1/4) = I₀/8.

questions.q: A progressive wave has frequency 50 Hz. Two points 0.40 m apart along the wave are the closest pair that oscillate 90° out of phase. What is the wave speed?
questions.x: 90° is a quarter of a cycle, so λ/4 = 0.40 m and λ = 1.6 m. v = fλ = 50 × 1.6 = 80 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: A stationary wave on a string at 200 Hz has adjacent nodes 0.30 m apart. What is the speed of the progressive waves on the string?
questions.x: Adjacent nodes are λ/2 apart, so λ = 0.60 m. v = fλ = 200 × 0.60 = 120 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: In a double-slit experiment, light of wavelength 600 nm passes through slits 0.50 mm apart onto a screen 2.0 m away. What is the fringe separation?
Light of wavelength 600 nm falls normally on a diffraction grating with 500 lines per mm. What is the total number of intensity maxima produced, including the zero order?
questions.x: d = 1/500 mm = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ m. n ≤ d/λ = 3.33, so n_max = 3 on each side. Total = 2(3) + 1 = 7.

questions.q: A pipe closed at one end has a fundamental frequency of 120 Hz. What is the next higher frequency at which it resonates?
questions.x: A closed pipe supports only odd harmonics (f, 3f, 5f…). The next one is 3 × 120 = 360 Hz.

questions.q: Two parallel plates 4.0 mm apart have a potential difference of 2000 V across them. What force acts on an electron between the plates?
A 470 μF capacitor is charged to 12 V. How much energy does it store?
questions.x: E = ½CV² = ½ × 470 × 10⁻⁶ × 12² = 0.034 J = 34 mJ. (68 mJ = CV² forgets the ½.)

questions.q: A 100 μF capacitor discharges through a 10 kΩ resistor. How long does the p.d. across it take to fall to half its initial value?
questions.x: τ = RC = 1.0 s. V = V₀e^(−t/τ) = V₀/2 gives t = τ ln 2 = 0.69 s.

questions.q: The electric field strength at 0.30 m from an isolated point charge is E. What is it at 0.10 m from the charge?
questions.x: For a point charge E ∝ 1/r². One third of the distance gives 9 times the field.

questions.q: A wire has resistance R. A second wire of the same material is twice as long and has half the diameter. What is its resistance?
questions.x: R = ρL/A. Half the diameter gives ¼ of the area. R′ = ρ(2L)/(A/4) = 8R.

questions.q: A copper wire of cross-sectional area 1.0 mm² carries 2.0 A. Copper has 8.5 × 10²⁸ free electrons per m³. What is the drift speed of the electrons?
A steady current of 5.0 mA flows for 2.0 minutes. How many electrons pass a point in the circuit?
A battery of e.m.f. 12 V and internal resistance 2.0 Ω is connected to a 4.0 Ω resistor. What is the terminal potential difference?

A 6.0 V supply with negligible internal resistance is connected across a 2.0 kΩ and a 4.0 kΩ resistor in series. A voltmeter of resistance 4.0 kΩ is connected across the 4.0 kΩ resistor. What does it read?
questions.x: 4.0 kΩ in parallel with 4.0 kΩ = 2.0 kΩ. The supply divides equally between 2.0 kΩ and 2.0 kΩ, giving 3.0 V (not the 4.0 V an ideal meter would read).

questions.q: A source has e.m.f. 6.0 V and internal resistance 3.0 Ω. What is the maximum power it can deliver to an external resistor?
questions.x: Maximum power transfer occurs when R = r = 3.0 Ω. I = 6.0/6.0 = 1.0 A, so P = I²R = 3.0 W.

questions.q: A wire 0.20 m long carries 3.0 A at 30° to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.050 T. What is the force on the wire?
An electron moving at 2.0 × 10⁷ m s⁻¹ enters a uniform magnetic field of 5.0 mT at right angles to the field. What is the radius of its circular path?
In a velocity selector, crossed fields have E = 3.0 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ and B = 0.015 T. Which ions pass through undeflected?
o: Only positive ions with speed 2.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹
Any ion with speed 2.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹, whatever its charge or mass
Any ion with speed 4.5 × 10² m s⁻¹
Only ions with a specific charge-to-mass ratio
questions.x: Undeflected when qE = qvB, so v = E/B = 2.0 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. The charge q cancels, so the sign, size of charge and mass don't matter.

questions.q: A coil of 200 turns and area 4.0 × 10⁻³ m² sits perpendicular to a magnetic field. The field falls uniformly from 0.30 T to zero in 0.10 s. What is the average induced e.m.f.?

A metal rod 0.50 m long moves at 4.0 m s⁻¹ at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 0.20 T, with the rod perpendicular to both the field and its velocity. What e.m.f. is induced across its ends?
A strong magnet dropped down a vertical copper tube falls much more slowly than in free fall. Why?
o: Copper is attracted to magnets, so the magnet sticks to the walls.
Air trapped in the tube is compressed.
Eddy currents induced in the tube produce a magnetic field that opposes the magnet's motion.
The magnet loses its magnetism inside the tube.
questions.x: The changing flux induces eddy currents in the copper. By Lenz's law their field opposes the change causing it, so it brakes the falling magnet. Copper is not ferromagnetic.

questions.q: A sinusoidal alternating voltage has a peak value of 340 V. What is its r.m.s. value?
An ideal transformer steps 240 V down to 12 V. The secondary current is 2.0 A. What is the primary current?
questions.x: Ideal transformer: VₚIₚ = VₛIₛ, so Iₚ = (12 × 2.0)/240 = 0.10 A.

questions.q: A sinusoidal current of peak value I₀ flows through a resistor of resistance R. What is the mean power dissipated?
questions.x: ⟨P⟩ = I_rms²R = (I₀/√2)²R = I₀²R/2.

questions.q: What is the energy of a photon of wavelength 500 nm?
Photons of energy 3.5 eV fall on a metal of work function 2.3 eV. What is the stopping potential?
questions.x: KE_max = hf − Φ = 3.5 − 2.3 = 1.2 eV. eV_s = KE_max, so V_s = 1.2 V.

questions.q: An electron starts from rest and is accelerated through a potential difference of 100 V. What is its de Broglie wavelength?
An electron is confined in a one-dimensional infinite potential well. What is the ratio (energy of the n = 3 state)/(energy of the ground state)?
questions.x: Eₙ = n²h²/(8mL²), so E ∝ n². E₃/E₁ = 9.

questions.q: In a photoelectric experiment, the intensity of the incident light is doubled while its frequency stays the same. What happens?
o: The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons doubles.
The rate of photoelectron emission doubles, and their maximum kinetic energy is unchanged.
questions.x: Intensity sets the number of photons per second, and so the emission rate. Each photon's energy hf is unchanged, so KE_max and the stopping potential stay the same.

questions.q: The activity of a radioactive sample falls from 800 Bq to 50 Bq in 24 days. What is its half-life?
A nucleus of uranium-238 (Z = 92) emits one α-particle and then two β⁻ particles. What is the resulting nucleus?
questions.x: α: A − 4, Z − 2, giving A = 234, Z = 90. Each β⁻ raises Z by 1, giving Z = 92. It is uranium-234.

questions.q: The mass defect of a helium-4 nucleus is 0.0304 u. What is its binding energy per nucleon?
questions.x: BE = 0.0304 × 931.5 = 28.3 MeV, shared by 4 nucleons: 7.1 MeV per nucleon.

questions.q: Which statement about nuclear fission of a heavy nucleus is correct?
o: The total binding energy of the products is less than that of the original nucleus.
The binding energy per nucleon of the products is greater than that of the original nucleus.
The total mass of the products is greater than the mass of the original nucleus.
Energy must be supplied continuously to keep the products apart.
questions.x: Fission moves nuclei towards the iron peak of the BE-per-nucleon curve. The products are more tightly bound, and the mass lost appears as released energy.
